title: Green Political Theory

cards.b:
Green political theory is the newest major ideology. It starts from one fact: economic growth on a finite planet has limits. It then asks how politics, economy and ethics must change.

It is rising in UPSC because it links Paper I theory with Paper II issues like climate justice and sustainable development.

Arne Naess coined the terms in 1973.

  • Shallow ecology (environmentalism): protect nature because it serves humans. Use technology and regulation.
  • Deep ecology (ecologism): nature has intrinsic value, humans are part of the web of life, so we need a basic change of worldview.

This is the anthropocentric versus ecocentric divide.
Heywood's summary: ecologism puts nature, not humans, at the centre.

The Club of Rome's Limits to Growth (1972) warned that resource use cannot rise forever. E.F. Schumacher, Small is Beautiful (1973), argued for human-scale, 'Buddhist' economics.

The Brundtland Report (1987) defined sustainable development as meeting present needs without compromising future generations. Greens say this still accepts growth, so it is a compromise.

Ecofeminists (Vandana Shiva, Maria Mies) link the domination of nature with the domination of women, both treated as resources. Murray Bookchin's social ecology says ecological crisis comes from social hierarchy, so the fix is decentralised, directly democratic communities.

Compare eco-socialism: capitalism is the root of the crisis.

Green parties arose in the 1970s-80s, e.g. Die Gruenen in West Germany (1980). Movements: Chipko, Greenpeace, Fridays for Future. Policies: carbon limits, renewable energy, degrowth, rights of nature (Ecuador's 2008 constitution).

Green theory also supports environmental justice: the poor suffer pollution most while the rich cause most of it.

Greens extend justice in two directions. Intergenerational justice: we hold the planet in trust for the unborn, a Burkean echo. Interspecies justice: animals and ecosystems have claims too, argued by Peter Singer (animal liberation, 1975) and Tom Regan (animal rights).

Legal moves include rights of nature: Ecuador (2008), and the 2017 Uttarakhand High Court order treating the Ganga and Yamuna as legal persons, later stayed by the Supreme Court.

• It is utopian: how to end growth in poor countries?
  • Eco-authoritarian risk: strong state to enforce limits.
  • Developing countries say the North grew by polluting and now restricts them.
  • Technology optimists believe innovation can decouple growth from damage.

Guha and Martinez-Alier's Varieties of Environmentalism (1997) argue that Northern deep ecology ignores the environmentalism of the poor in the South, such as forest and water struggles.

Gandhi's line 'the earth provides enough for everyone's need but not for everyone's greed' is the standard quote. Chipko (1973, Uttarakhand), Narmada Bachao Andolan, and Ramachandra Guha's Environmentalism: A Global History and the idea of 'environmentalism of the poor' (Guha and Martinez-Alier) are central.

India's stance in climate talks: common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR). The Mission LiFE call (2022) stresses lifestyle change.

"Distinguish shallow and deep ecology."
"Examine green political theory as a challenge to modern ideologies."
"Is sustainable development a contradiction in terms?"

Structure: state the ecological premise, deep vs shallow, principles, thinkers, critiques, link to Gandhi, Chipko and CBDR.

Sample line for the answer: Arne Naess coined 'deep ecology' in 1973, asking whether human-centred values themselves need to change, while shallow ecology seeks reform within industrial society.
